title: I let Claude Code make a complete Dog's Dinner of my game. Three weeks later it's on Steam.
author: njbmartin
selftext:
I'm making A Dog's Dinner, a management sim where you run a fresh dog food company. You start cooking in your flat for a few dogs down the street: cook, portion, freeze, and pack the boxes before the 2pm van. Then you hire people, design recipes, and eventually move into a warehouse and build it out. It's coming to Steam in Early Access, playable from the first day in the flat to the 18,000-customer goal, with full controller support on the Steam Deck.

The first commit was 20 October. Claude Code agents have done most of the making since: the code, and also the art, the Steam images, the trailer, the music, the sound effects and the voiceover. The direction and the taste are mine.

I went back through my own messages to see how much I actually did. In 21 days I sent about 700 messages, and most were a sentence or less. By my rough count I was actively at it for about 3 hours a day, mostly playing builds on the Steam Deck and saying what didn't work.

The rest of the time the agents work through a queue of GitHub issues on their own. So far that's about 100,000 lines of game code, 59,000 lines of tests and 116 issues closed.

Roughly how it went:

* **Day 1:** I talked the design through with it. A fresh agent poked holes in the doc, and four made-up players (a tycoon veteran, a cosy player, a business-sim nerd and an Early Access streamer) reviewed it. The agents then built a greybox prototype and kept going. By the end of the day there was building, the dog, subscribers, recipes and 150 workers walking around.
* **Day 2:** the career and the money side: loans, investors, leases.
* **Day 7:** the first trailer storyboard.
* **Day 9:** the first Steam upload, the store art and the store page copy.
* **Day 14:** submitted for Early Access.
* **Since then:** mostly playtesting on the Deck and fixing what I find.

Bigger features start as a design doc. Before I see it, a separate agent reads it as if it had to build from it and lists what it would still need to know. Most of that gets settled without me, and I only get the questions that are really mine. Then it becomes a plan of small tasks. Each task goes to a fresh agent that writes the test first, builds it, runs about 2,600 tests and writes a report. Those tests run in a few minutes without opening Unity, because the game's simulation is plain C# kept separate from the engine. A different agent reviews the diff against the task. Only the diff, the task and the report, nothing else. This week a reviewer caught a test that would have passed even with the feature deleted, because both values it compared were clamped to the same floor. The fix went back to the agent that wrote it, and a third agent checked just the fix.

The agents can't watch the game the way I do, so the game has capture runs: scripted sessions that start the game with nobody at the keyboard, play through a scene, and save screenshots at Steam Deck size. That's how the agents see their own changes.

Anything a player will see also gets looked at as three different players: a cosy player, an optimiser who wants the best numbers, and someone who'll quit in the first 30 seconds if it's confusing. A UI designer and a copywriter look too. The agents go through the screenshots as each of them. What bores them, what confuses them, what would make them come back. Then they fix what they find. That one came from me early on, after a build that was playable but I found boring by day 12.

A task takes 20–45 minutes. When a feature's done, a script runs about 3,000 Unity tests (around 18 minutes) and uploads to the Steam playtest branch only if they all pass.

The other stuff:

Everything you see is built in code at runtime, the people and dogs from blobby shapes, the kit from rounded boxes. I picked the style from a page of options it made for me. The Steam capsules are rendered from scenes inside the game. The trailer is real footage filmed by scripts that play the game, cut together with HyperFrames (HTML to video). Music, sound effects and Biscuit's voice in the trailer are ElevenLabs. It made several takes of everything and put them on an audition page, I picked, and it wired them in.

The bit I check most is the dev diary. From the very first session it's kept a log of everything it does, including what failed and how it fixed it, and it publishes it as a page I can read on my phone. It's up to 133 entries now. Every screenshot is kept too, rejected ones included, which is about 26,000 images. When I come back to it I read the diary rather than ask what happened.

More than happy to answer any questions!

Wishlist on Steam: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/5502930/A\_Dogs\_Dinner/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5502930/A_Dogs_Dinner/)
